stem: You are trimming a project `CLAUDE.md`. Following the official guidance, which line should you cut?

options.text: Run `pnpm test:unit --runInBand`; the parallel run deadlocks on CI
options.why: A command Claude cannot guess, plus the reason for it. This is exactly what belongs in CLAUDE.md.

options.text: Branch names follow `feat/<ticket>-<slug>`
options.why: Repository etiquette such as branch naming is on the docs' list of things to include.

options.text: Write clean, readable code and follow JavaScript best practices
options.why: Self-evident advice Claude already follows. It costs tokens every session and changes nothing, so it should go.

options.text: `DATABASE_URL` must point at the local Docker Postgres on port 5433
options.why: A developer-environment quirk that is not obvious from the code. The docs list these as worth keeping.

explanation: CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session, so each line is a recurring cost. The test from the best-practices page is: "Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?" Keep commands Claude cannot guess, style rules that differ from defaults, repo etiquette, environment quirks and gotchas. Cut standard conventions, self-evident practices, file-by-file descriptions and anything Claude can learn by reading the code.
reference: Claude Code docs: Best practices (Write an effective CLAUDE.md)

stem: In Claude Code, `/compact` and `/clear` both leave you with an empty context; the only difference is that `/compact` saves the old conversation first.

options.text: True
options.why: `/compact` keeps the same conversation going. It replaces the history with a summary rather than emptying it.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct. `/compact` summarizes the conversation so far and carries on with that summary. `/clear` starts a new conversation with empty context.

explanation: Use `/compact [instructions]` to free space while continuing the same task. You can steer the summary, for example `/compact focus on the auth bug fix`. Use `/clear` between unrelated tasks, because old conversation crowds out what you need next. The cleared conversation is not deleted: you can get it back with `/resume`.
reference: Claude Code docs: Commands; Explore the context window

stem: You want personal, project-specific instructions for Claude Code (your sandbox URL, your preferred test data) that load next to the team's `CLAUDE.md` but are not committed. What is the file name you create at the project root?
explanation: `CLAUDE.local.md` loads alongside `CLAUDE.md` and is treated the same way. Within each directory it is appended after `CLAUDE.md`, so your personal notes are read last at that level. Add it to `.gitignore` so it stays out of version control. In the Agent SDK it loads only when `settingSources` includes `"local"`.
reference: Claude Code docs: How Claude remembers your project

stem: You want a project skill that the whole team gets from git and that anyone can run by typing `/deploy`. Where do you put it?

options.text: A `## deploy` section in a `SKILLS.md` file at the repository root
options.why: Claude Code does not read a `SKILLS.md` file. Each skill is its own directory holding a `SKILL.md`.

options.text: `.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md`
options.why: Project skills live in `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. The directory name (or the frontmatter `name`) becomes the command.

options.text: A `skills.deploy` entry in `.claude/settings.json`
options.why: Skills are files on disk, not settings keys. Settings can hide or show skills (`skillOverrides`) but cannot define one.

options.text: `~/.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md`
options.why: That is a personal skill. It works in all your projects but lives in your home directory, so teammates never get it from git.

explanation: A skill is a directory with a `SKILL.md`: YAML frontmatter (at least a `description`) and then markdown instructions. Its location decides who gets it: `~/.claude/skills/` for you on this machine, `.claude/skills/` for everyone in the repo, a plugin's `skills/` for wherever the plugin is enabled (as `/plugin-name:skill-name`). The older `.claude/commands/deploy.md` format still works and also creates `/deploy`.
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills

stem: You open Claude Code in a repository that has no `CLAUDE.md`. Which command makes Claude analyse the codebase and write a starter `CLAUDE.md` with the build commands, test instructions and conventions it finds?

options.text: `/memory`
options.why: `/memory` lists memory files and opens one in your editor (creating an empty file if needed). It does not analyse the codebase.

options.text: `/context`
options.why: `/context` shows how the context window is being used, including which memory files loaded. It writes nothing.

options.text: `/config`
options.why: `/config` opens the settings panel for options such as theme and output style.

options.text: `/init`
options.why: `/init` explores the project and generates a starting `CLAUDE.md`. If one already exists, it suggests improvements instead of overwriting.

explanation: `/init` gives you a first draft. Then refine it with what Claude could not discover on its own. With `CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1` set, `/init` runs an interactive flow that can also set up skills and hooks. Run `/context` afterwards to confirm the file appears under Memory files.
reference: Claude Code docs: How Claude remembers your project

stem: Match each Claude Code command with the situation it is for.

options.text: `/clear`
options.why: Starts a new conversation with empty context.

options.text: `/compact`
options.why: Summarizes the conversation so far and continues with the summary.

options.text: `/context`
options.why: Shows context usage as a grid, including which memory files loaded.

options.text: `/memory`
options.why: Opens CLAUDE.md files for editing and toggles auto memory.

prompts.text: You finished the payments bug and are starting unrelated work on the docs site
Halfway through a long refactor, the context is filling up and you want to keep going
You want to check whether your new `CLAUDE.md` actually loaded and how much space it takes
You want to edit your user-level `CLAUDE.md` and turn auto memory off

explanation: Context is the main resource to manage in Claude Code. `/clear` between unrelated tasks, `/compact` (optionally with focus instructions) to keep going on the same task, `/context` to see what is using space and which instruction files loaded, and `/memory` to open and edit memory files.
reference: Claude Code docs: Commands

stem: You want Claude Code to plan with Opus while in plan mode, then switch automatically to Sonnet to write the code. Which model setting does that?

options.text: `best`
options.why: `best` picks the strongest model available to you (Fable where available, otherwise Opus) for the whole session. It does not switch by mode.

options.text: `opusplan`
options.why: `opusplan` uses `opus` in plan mode and switches to `sonnet` for execution.

options.text: `opus[1m]`
options.why: This asks for Opus with a 1M-token context window. It stays on Opus for everything.

options.text: `default`
options.why: `default` clears any override and goes back to the runtime default for your account. It is not a hybrid mode.

explanation: Aliases such as `opus`, `sonnet` and `haiku` resolve to a recommended version for your provider and move over time. Use a full model name such as `claude-opus-5-5` to pin a version. `opusplan` is a special alias for the plan-then-execute pattern.
reference: Claude Code docs: Model configuration

stem: On current Claude Code (v2.1.277 or later), a repository that has an `AGENTS.md` and no `CLAUDE.md` or `CLAUDE.local.md` anywhere on the path gets its `AGENTS.md` read as project instructions, with no import or setting needed.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct. By default Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` when no `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md` or `CLAUDE.local.md` exists in the working directory or above it.

options.text: False
options.why: An `@AGENTS.md` import inside a `CLAUDE.md` used to be required. Since v2.1.277 Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` directly when no CLAUDE file counts.

explanation: The default **Project instructions** value is `claude-md-or-agents-md`: CLAUDE files if any exist on the path, otherwise `AGENTS.md`. Your `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, the managed CLAUDE.md and `.claude/rules/` do not count for that check. To read both files, set **Project instructions** to `claude-md-and-agents-md`. An existing `CLAUDE.md` that contains `@AGENTS.md` keeps working and never loads the file twice.
reference: Claude Code docs: How Claude remembers your project (AGENTS.md)

stem: Your `~/.claude/settings.json` sets `"spinnerTipsEnabled": false`, but the team's committed `.claude/settings.json` sets it to `true`, so you see tips in that project. How do you turn them off for yourself in this project without changing anything for your teammates?

options.text: Add `"spinnerTipsEnabled": false` again to `~/.claude/settings.json`
options.why: User settings are the lowest level. The shared project file sits above them and still wins.

options.text: Change the value in the committed `.claude/settings.json`
options.why: That turns tips off for everyone who pulls the change, which is not what you want.

options.text: Add `"spinnerTipsEnabled": false` to `.claude/settings.local.json`
options.why: Project local sits above shared project, and the file stays out of git, so only your sessions change.

options.text: Export an environment variable for the key before running `claude`
options.why: Environment variables are not a level in the settings stack, and only some keys have a paired variable. This key is a settings value.

explanation: From highest to lowest: managed settings, `--settings` on the command line, `.claude/settings.local.json`, `.claude/settings.json`, `~/.claude/settings.json`. A key set higher overrides the same key lower down. The local file is for personal overrides in one project. Claude Code adds it to your global git excludes when it first writes the file. If you create it by hand, add it to `.gitignore` yourself.
reference: Claude Code docs: Settings files and precedence

stem: The same settings key is set in every one of these places. Order them from the one whose value wins to the one with the lowest precedence.

options.text: Managed settings deployed by your organisation
JSON passed with `claude --settings` at launch
`.claude/settings.local.json`
`.claude/settings.json`
`~/.claude/settings.json`

explanation: Nothing in your own files or `--settings` overrides a managed key. `--settings` applies for one session, above every file except managed. Then come project local (personal, gitignored), shared project (committed) and user. Two cautions: list keys such as `permissions.allow` merge across levels instead of overriding, and some keys have their own flag or environment variable that decides things per key, outside this stack.
reference: Claude Code docs: Settings files and precedence

stem: A `deploy` skill pushes to production. You want people to be able to run it with `/deploy`, but Claude must never decide on its own to deploy because the code "looks ready". Which frontmatter does that?

options.text: `user-invocable: false`
options.why: This is the opposite: it hides the skill from the `/` menu so only Claude can invoke it.

options.text: `disable-model-invocation: true`
options.why: Claude cannot invoke the skill on its own, and its description is kept out of Claude's context. You can still type `/deploy`.

options.text: `context: fork`
options.why: This runs the skill in a separate subagent. It changes where the skill runs, not who may start it.

options.text: `allowed-tools:` left empty so Claude has no tools to deploy with
options.why: `allowed-tools` pre-approves tools for the turn. Leaving it empty does not stop Claude from invoking the skill.

explanation: By default both you and Claude can invoke any skill. Use `disable-model-invocation: true` for workflows with side effects or where you control the timing (`/commit`, `/deploy`). If Claude tries anyway, Claude Code blocks the call. Use `user-invocable: false` for background knowledge that Claude should apply but that is not a meaningful command for a user.
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills (Control who invokes a skill)

stem: You start Claude Code at a repository root that has a `CLAUDE.md`, a `packages/api/CLAUDE.md`, a rule with `paths: ["src/api/**"]`, and a skill whose folder holds `SKILL.md` and `reference.md`. Before you type anything, which of these are already in Claude's context? (Choose two.)

options.text: The root `CLAUDE.md`
options.why: CLAUDE.md files in the working directory and above it load at launch.

options.text: The skill's name and description
options.why: Skill descriptions load at startup so Claude knows what is available. That is the first layer of progressive disclosure.

options.text: The full body of `SKILL.md`
options.why: The body loads only when you or Claude invoke the skill.

options.text: The skill's `reference.md`
options.why: Supporting files load only when Claude decides to read them while running the skill.

options.text: `packages/api/CLAUDE.md`
options.why: CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories load on demand, once Claude reads or edits a file in that subdirectory.

options.text: The path-scoped API rule
options.why: A rule with `paths` loads only when Claude works with a matching file.

explanation: At startup Claude Code loads always-on content: CLAUDE.md files from the working directory up, unscoped rules, auto memory, and skill descriptions. Everything else loads when it becomes relevant: skill bodies on invocation, supporting files on demand, nested CLAUDE.md files and path-scoped rules when Claude touches matching files. This is why long reference material belongs in skills and scoped rules, not in the root CLAUDE.md.
reference: Claude Code docs: How Claude remembers your project; Extend Claude with skills

stem:
A skill's `SKILL.md` contains this line:

```markdown
## Current changes
!`git diff HEAD`
```

What happens when the skill is invoked?

options.text: Claude sees the line as an instruction and runs `git diff HEAD` with its Bash tool when it gets to that step
options.why: The command runs before Claude sees the skill at all. Claude never receives the command, only its output.

options.text: Claude Code runs it first and inlines the output before Claude sees the skill
options.why: This is dynamic context injection: the output is inlined into the skill content, so Claude starts with the real diff.

options.text: Claude Code asks you to approve `git diff HEAD`, then sends the output as a separate tool result
options.why: Injected commands never prompt. They are checked against permission rules, and a command that is not allowed aborts the invocation.

options.text: Nothing runs; `!` lines are only expanded for skills shipped inside plugins
options.why: Injection works for personal, project, plugin and additional-directory skills. Skills synced from claude.ai are the exception.

explanation: The `` !`command` `` form (or a fenced block opened with ` ```! `) runs a shell command while the skill renders. Its output replaces the placeholder as plain text, and the output is not re-scanned for further placeholders. Use it to ground a skill in live data. Because it runs a command on your machine, review it as you would a script. Admins can turn it off with `disableSkillShellExecution`.
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills (Inject dynamic context)

stem: A `CLAUDE.md` imports `@docs/a.md`, which imports another file, which imports another, and so on. What is the maximum number of import hops Claude Code follows? Type a number.
explanation: Imported files can import other files recursively, up to four hops. Relative import paths resolve against the file that contains the import, not the working directory. Imports help you organise instructions but do not save context, because imported files load at launch along with the file that imports them.
reference: Claude Code docs: How Claude remembers your project (Import additional files)

stem: In a skill body, which placeholder expands to the whole argument string you typed after the command, so that `/fix-issue 123` turns `Fix GitHub issue <placeholder>` into `Fix GitHub issue 123`?
explanation: `$ARGUMENTS` holds the full argument string. `$ARGUMENTS[N]` and the shorthand `$N` pick one argument by 0-based index, using shell-style quoting. Names declared in the `arguments` frontmatter become `$name`. If you pass arguments and no placeholder receives them, Claude Code appends `ARGUMENTS: <value>` to the skill content so Claude still sees them.
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills (Pass arguments to skills)

stem: In a TypeScript Agent SDK app, you want sessions to use the built-in Explanatory output style. Which option does it?

options.text: `outputStyle: "Explanatory"` as a top-level `Options` field
options.why: `Options` has no `outputStyle` field. TypeScript rejects it as an unknown property.

options.text: `systemPrompt: { type: "preset", preset: "explanatory" }`
options.why: The only system prompt preset is `claude_code`. Output styles are a separate settings value.

options.text: `settings: { outputStyle: "Explanatory" }`
options.why: `outputStyle` is a settings key. The inline `settings` object (or a settings file path) is where the SDK accepts it.

options.text: `env: { CLAUDE_OUTPUT_STYLE: "Explanatory" }`
options.why: Output styles are chosen through the `outputStyle` setting, not an environment variable.

explanation: Output styles change Claude's role, tone and format for every response. In Claude Code you pick one with `/output-style` or `/config`, which saves `outputStyle` to `.claude/settings.local.json`. In the SDK, pass it through `settings` (an object in TypeScript; a JSON string or file path in Python), or put it in a settings file that your `settingSources` load.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Modifying system prompts (Output styles)

stem: Your repo has a plugin at `./plugins/review-kit` containing `skills/check/SKILL.md`. In an Agent SDK app, how do you load the plugin, and what prompt runs that skill directly?

options.text: `plugins: [{ type: "local", path: "./plugins/review-kit" }]`, then send `/review-kit:check`
options.why: `local` is the only plugin type the SDK accepts, and plugin skills are namespaced as `plugin-name:skill-name`.

options.text: `plugins: [{ type: "marketplace", path: "review-kit" }]`, then send `/review-kit:check`
options.why: The SDK takes local paths only. To use a marketplace plugin, download it and point at its directory.

options.text: `settingSources: ["project"]` loads the plugin automatically, then send `/check@review-kit`
options.why: A plugin folder in the repo is not picked up by setting sources, and `@` is not how plugin skills are named.

options.text: `skills: ["review-kit/*"]` loads the plugin's skills, then send `/review-kit/check`
options.why: The `skills` option filters skills that are already loaded. It takes exact names only and rejects wildcards.

explanation: A plugin bundles skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers as one unit. In the SDK you pass local directories in `plugins`. Relative paths resolve against `cwd`, and the path must be the plugin root, the parent of `skills/` or `.claude-plugin/`. Confirm loading in the `system`/`init` message: `plugins` lists them, and `skills` and `slash_commands` show names such as `review-kit:check`.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Plugins in the SDK

stem: Splitting a 600-line `CLAUDE.md` into a short file that `@imports` five topic files reduces how much context the instructions use in each session.

options.text: True
options.why: Imported files are expanded and loaded at launch along with the importing file, so the total cost does not change.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct. Imports help organisation, not context cost. To actually load less, use path-scoped rules, nested CLAUDE.md files or skills, which load on demand.

explanation: The docs suggest keeping each CLAUDE.md under about 200 lines, because longer files use more context and reduce adherence. Content that matters only for part of the codebase belongs in `.claude/rules/` files with `paths` frontmatter or in a subdirectory `CLAUDE.md`. Multi-step procedures belong in skills. Plain `@imports` only rearrange text that still loads every session.
reference: Claude Code docs: How Claude remembers your project (Write effective instructions)

stem: Match each built-in Claude Code output style with the developer it suits.

options.text: Proactive
options.why: Starts work right away and makes reasonable assumptions instead of asking about routine decisions.

options.text: Concise
options.why: Leads with the result and leaves out preamble, narration and recaps.

options.text: Explanatory
options.why: Adds short Insight blocks explaining the choices behind the code.

options.text: Learning
options.why: Explains choices and leaves `TODO(human)` pieces for you to write.

prompts.text: "Stop asking me which file name to use; pick something sensible and I'll correct you"
"Your answers are too long; just tell me what happened"
A new joiner who wants the reasoning behind each change while the work still gets done
A junior who wants hands-on practice writing the tricky parts themselves

explanation: Each built-in style keeps Claude Code's default engineering instructions and adds its own. Styles are instructions, not guarantees. Proactive does not change your permission mode, so permission prompts still appear. Explanatory's Insight blocks appear in the conversation, not as comments in your files.
reference: Claude Code docs: Output styles

stem:
An SDK agent should use the team's `.claude/skills/code-review/SKILL.md`, but Claude never invokes it, and the skill is missing from the `skills` array in the init message. The options are:

```ts
{
  cwd: repoRoot,
  settingSources: [],
  skills: "all",
  allowedTools: ["Read", "Grep"],
}
```

What is wrong?

options.text: `allowedTools` does not include `"Skill"`, so Claude cannot call the Skill tool
options.why: When `skills` is set, the SDK adds the Skill tool to `allowedTools` for you.

options.text: `settingSources: []` disables filesystem discovery, so the skill is never found
options.why: Skills are discovered through the `user` and `project` sources. With none loaded, `"all"` enables every skill in an empty set.

options.text: `skills: "all"` is invalid; list the skill as `["code-review"]` instead
options.why: `"all"` is the documented way to enable every discovered skill. The list form would not help, because nothing is discovered.

options.text: `cwd` must point at `repoRoot/.claude/skills`
options.why: `cwd` should be the project directory. The SDK looks for `.claude/skills/` there and in parent directories up to the repo root.

explanation: The `skills` option filters skills that were discovered; it does not load any by itself. Discovery comes from `settingSources`: `"project"` for `.claude/skills/` (and directories added with `additionalDirectories`), `"user"` for `~/.claude/skills/`. To load skills from a specific path without filesystem settings, use the `plugins` option. The SDK has no programmatic API for registering a skill.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Extend agents with skills (Troubleshooting)

stem: After months of use, a repo's auto memory index `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md` has grown to about 400 one-line entries. Claude reliably recalls the older preferences but seems to have no idea about the newer ones at the start of a session. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Auto memory is per worktree, and the newer entries were saved from a different worktree
options.why: All worktrees and subdirectories of the same git repository share one auto memory directory.

options.text: Auto memory loads only when you run `/memory`, so the newer entries were never read
options.why: Auto memory loads at the start of every session. `/memory` is for browsing and editing it.

options.text: Claude Code deletes memory entries older than `cleanupPeriodDays`
options.why: The opposite of the symptom, and also untrue: memory files are excluded from the transcript retention sweep.

options.text: Only the first 200 lines or 25KB of `MEMORY.md` load at session start
options.why: Content past the threshold is not loaded. The index should stay short, with detail moved into topic files that Claude reads on demand.

explanation: `MEMORY.md` is an index: Claude Code loads its first 200 lines or 25KB, whichever comes first, and Claude reads topic files such as `feedback_testing.md` when it needs them. When the index nears the limit, Claude Code reminds Claude to shorten it. When it is over the limit, the write still succeeds but Claude is told to rewrite the index. CLAUDE.md files have no such line limit (files over 4 MiB are skipped), but shorter files are followed more reliably.
reference: Claude Code docs: How Claude remembers your project (Auto memory)

stem: Two hours into a session, Claude Code auto-compacts. Which of these still reach Claude in full right after compaction, without Claude touching any particular file? (Choose two.)

options.text: The project-root `CLAUDE.md`
options.why: It is re-read from disk and re-injected after compaction.

options.text: The active output style
options.why: The system prompt and output style still apply after compaction.

options.text: "Always use `pnpm`", which you typed in chat 40 turns ago
options.why: Instructions given only in conversation are summarized with everything else and can be lost. Put them in CLAUDE.md to make them persist.

options.text: A `paths:`-scoped rule that loaded earlier when Claude edited a matching file
options.why: It loaded into message history, so compaction summarizes it away. It comes back only when Claude touches a matching file again.

options.text: A subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` that loaded on demand an hour ago
options.why: Nested CLAUDE.md files also reload on demand, not automatically after compaction.

explanation: What survives depends on how content was loaded. The system prompt and output style still apply. Project-root CLAUDE.md, unscoped rules and auto memory are re-injected from disk. On-demand content (path-scoped rules, nested CLAUDE.md files) and anything said in chat lives in message history and gets summarized. If a scoped rule must persist, drop its `paths:` or move it to the root CLAUDE.md. A `SessionStart` hook matching the `compact` source can also re-inject context.
reference: Claude Code docs: Explore the context window (What survives compaction)

stem: A repository keeps all agent instructions in `AGENTS.md` and has no `CLAUDE.md`. Claude Code followed them fine until a developer created a gitignored `CLAUDE.local.md` with two personal notes. Now, for that developer only, Claude seems unaware of everything in `AGENTS.md`. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Local files have higher precedence than project files, so `CLAUDE.local.md` overrides `AGENTS.md` line by line
options.why: Instruction files are concatenated, not overridden key by key. The issue is which files get loaded at all.

options.text: `CLAUDE.local.md` counts as a CLAUDE file, so by default `AGENTS.md` is skipped
options.why: Under the default `claude-md-or-agents-md`, any `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/CLAUDE.md` or `CLAUDE.local.md` on the path means CLAUDE files only.

options.text: Claude Code never reads `AGENTS.md` directly; it was being read only because Claude chose to open it
options.why: Since v2.1.277 Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` directly as project instructions when no CLAUDE file counts.

options.text: Gitignored files disable every instruction file that is tracked by git
options.why: Whether a file is tracked by git has no effect on loading. Only which instruction files exist matters.

explanation: This trap is documented: adding a `CLAUDE.local.md` to an AGENTS.md-only project stops `AGENTS.md` from loading for you. Fixes: set **Project instructions** to `claude-md-and-agents-md` (in `/config`, or under `pluginConfigs` for `cc-plugin-agents-md@builtin` in user settings), or put an `@AGENTS.md` import in a CLAUDE file. To check what loaded, look for the path in `/memory`.
reference: Claude Code docs: How Claude remembers your project (When Claude Code reads AGENTS.md)

stem: A `commit` skill has `allowed-tools: Bash(git add *) Bash(git commit *)` in its frontmatter. Which statements about that field are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: During the turn that invokes the skill, Claude can run matching `git add` and `git commit` commands without a permission prompt
options.why: That is the field's purpose: it pre-approves the listed tools for the invoking turn.

options.text: The grant ends when you send your next message, even though the skill's instructions stay in context
options.why: Instructions persist across turns; permissions do not. Invoking the skill again re-applies the grant.

options.text: While the skill is active, every tool not listed becomes unavailable to Claude
options.why: `allowed-tools` does not restrict anything. All tools stay callable under your normal permission settings. Use `disallowed-tools` to remove tools.

options.text: It overrides a `Bash(git commit *)` deny rule in project settings while the skill runs
options.why: Deny and ask rules still take precedence. The field only removes prompts for calls that would otherwise ask.

options.text: The grant lasts for the rest of the session once the skill has been invoked
options.why: It lasts for the invoking turn only. For a session-wide grant, add allow rules to your permission settings.

explanation: Keep two lifecycles apart. The rendered skill content enters the conversation once and stays. The `allowed-tools` grant applies only to the turn that invoked the skill. The field also pre-approves the skill's own `!` injected commands, which is why repository skills deserve review: workspace trust does not gate it, and an org can ignore it with `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`.
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills (Pre-approve tools for a skill)

stem: Match each requirement with the Claude Code mechanism that fits it best.

options.text: CLAUDE.md
options.why: Always-loaded facts and conventions, followed as guidance.

options.text: A skill
options.why: A reusable procedure or reference that loads only when invoked or relevant.

options.text: A hook
options.why: Code the harness runs at a lifecycle event, every time, whatever Claude decides.

options.text: A subagent
options.why: A separate context with its own prompt and tools that returns only a summary.

prompts.text: Every session should know that tests run with `make test` and API handlers live in `src/api/handlers/`
A 12-step release checklist that matters only when someone is cutting a release
Prettier must run after every file edit, with no exceptions
Read 80 log files to find a root cause without flooding the main conversation

explanation: CLAUDE.md is advisory context that is always loaded. Skills keep procedures out of context until needed. Hooks are deterministic, so anything that must happen goes there. Subagents keep large reads in their own context window. Each mechanism goes wrong when misused: a checklist in CLAUDE.md costs tokens every session, a must-run rule in CLAUDE.md can be skipped, and a subagent does not see your conversation history.
reference: Claude Code docs: Use Claude Code features in the SDK (Choose the right feature); Output styles

stem: Several skills and commands share the name `deploy`. Which statements about what `/deploy` runs are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: With `deploy` in both `~/.claude/skills/` and the project's `.claude/skills/`, `/deploy` runs the personal one
options.why: Name resolution goes enterprise over personal over project, so the personal skill wins.

options.text: With `.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md` and `.claude/commands/deploy.md`, `/deploy` runs the skill
options.why: When a skill and a command file share a name, the skill wins.

options.text: The project skill wins over the personal one because it is more specific to the repository
options.why: Unlike settings, skill name resolution puts personal above project.

options.text: An enabled plugin with a `deploy` skill replaces the project's `deploy` skill
options.why: Both load. Plugin skills are namespaced, so the plugin's one runs as `/plugin-name:deploy`.

options.text: A nested `apps/web/.claude/skills/deploy` replaces the root `deploy` skill
options.why: Both stay available. `/deploy` runs the root skill and `/apps/web:deploy` runs the nested one.

explanation: Interviewers like this one because skill resolution is the reverse of settings intuition. For settings, project beats user. For skills with the same name, enterprise beats personal beats project. Skills beat legacy command files. Plugin and nested skills avoid collisions by being namespaced or directory-qualified.
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills (Resolve skills that share a name)

stem: You work in `monorepo/apps/web`. Claude Code also loads `monorepo/CLAUDE.md`, which the platform team wrote for Go services and which keeps steering Claude wrong in your TypeScript app. You want to skip that one file for yourself only, without changing anything that is committed. What do you do?

options.text: Add `monorepo/CLAUDE.md` to your `.gitignore`
options.why: Git ignore rules affect commits, not what Claude Code loads. The file is still on disk and still loads.

options.text: Launch with `--setting-sources user,local` so project-level instructions are skipped for your sessions
options.why: This drops every project source, including your app's own CLAUDE.md, rules, settings and skills, not just the one file.

options.text: Put "Ignore the parent CLAUDE.md" in `apps/web/CLAUDE.md`
options.why: Both files are concatenated into context, and this is only a request. Claude may still follow either one.

options.text: Add the file's path pattern to `claudeMdExcludes` in `.claude/settings.local.json`
options.why: `claudeMdExcludes` skips matching CLAUDE.md and rules files by glob on absolute paths, and the local file keeps the change personal.

explanation: `claudeMdExcludes` exists for monorepos where ancestor instruction files do not apply to you. Patterns match absolute paths with glob syntax. You can set it at any settings layer, and arrays merge across layers. The one file it cannot exclude is a managed (organisation) CLAUDE.md.
reference: Claude Code docs: How Claude remembers your project (Exclude specific CLAUDE.md files)

stem: A `pdf-forms` skill folder holds `SKILL.md` and a large `reference.md`. A user asks Claude to fill in a PDF form. Put the steps of progressive disclosure in the order they happen.

options.text: At session start, only the skill's name and description are listed in Claude's context
Claude matches the request to the description and calls the Skill tool
Claude Code renders `SKILL.md` (running any `!` commands) and adds the body to the conversation as one message
Claude opens `reference.md` with its file tools because the instructions point there for field mappings

explanation: Three layers keep skills cheap: the description (always listed, truncated at 1,536 characters together with `when_to_use`), the body (loaded on invocation and then kept in context across turns), and supporting files (read only when needed). This is why the docs say to keep `SKILL.md` under 500 lines, to link detailed material from it, and to put the key use case first in the description.
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills

stem: A developer adds `"outputStyle": "explanatory"` to `~/.claude/settings.json`. No project file sets `outputStyle`. Claude Code starts with no error, but responses never include Insight blocks. Why?

options.text: `outputStyle` is honoured only in `.claude/settings.local.json`
options.why: It can be set at any settings level. Setting it in user settings is the documented way to make a style your default everywhere.

options.text: The value is case-sensitive; `explanatory` matches no style, so the Default style applies
options.why: Settings must use the exact names (`Proactive`, `Concise`, `Explanatory`, `Learning`). Only the `/output-style` command ignores case.

options.text: Built-in styles must be copied into `~/.claude/output-styles/` before settings can refer to them
options.why: Built-in styles need no files. That directory is for custom styles.

options.text: Output styles apply only after `/clear`, so the running session ignores the change
options.why: Since v2.1.251 a style change applies from your next message. The real problem is the value itself.

explanation: A wrong-case or misspelled `outputStyle` fails silently and gives you the Default style. Write `Explanatory`, or run `/output-style explanatory`, which ignores case and saves the correct value to `.claude/settings.local.json`. If a project's own settings set `outputStyle`, they override your user default.
reference: Claude Code docs: Output styles (Change your output style)

stem: An SDK app passes `skills: ["pdf"]`, and the project also contains a `deploy` skill. Which statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: `deploy` is left out of the model's skill listing, and the Skill tool rejects it if Claude tries to call it
options.why: Unlisted skills are hidden and rejected with a "not in this session's skills allowlist" error.

options.text: Sending the prompt `/deploy` still runs the skill
options.why: Dispatch by name does not depend on the `skills` option. A user-invocable skill runs when you send its command.

options.text: Claude can no longer read `.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md` with Read or Bash
options.why: The option is a context filter, not a sandbox. The files stay on disk and readable, so do not store secrets in them.

options.text: `skills: ["pdf", "ops:*"]` would also enable every skill from the `ops` plugin
options.why: Wildcards are rejected before the session starts. List each skill by its exact name, or use `"all"`.

options.text: You must also add `"Skill"` to `allowedTools` or `pdf` cannot run
options.why: Setting `skills` adds the Skill tool for you. Only an explicit `tools` list needs `"Skill"` added by hand.

explanation: `skills` takes `"all"`, an exact-name list (`plugin:skill` for plugin skills), or `[]`. Leaving it out keeps CLI behaviour; it does not mean skills are off. It controls what the model may invoke, not what a user can dispatch, and it is no security boundary for the files themselves. The init message's `skills` array lists the same user-invocable skills whether or not they are in your list.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Extend agents with skills

stem: The committed `.claude/settings.json` has `"permissions": { "allow": ["Bash(npm test *)"] }`. A developer, who wants `npm test` to prompt again for their own sessions, puts `"permissions": { "allow": ["Bash(make *)"] }` in `.claude/settings.local.json`, expecting it to replace the team's list. What actually happens?

options.text: Only `Bash(make *)` is allowed, because the local file overrides the shared file
options.why: Override by precedence applies to scalar keys. List keys such as `permissions.allow` merge instead.

options.text: Only `Bash(npm test *)` is allowed, because committed project rules win over local ones
options.why: Local sits above shared project. The real point is that the two lists merge, so neither is dropped.

options.text: Both rules apply, because `permissions.allow` arrays from every settings file are combined
options.why: Lists merge across files, so each file can add entries without removing another's. To make `npm test` prompt again, add an `ask` rule; removing an allow rule will not work.

options.text: Claude Code reports a Settings Warning about conflicting allow lists and ignores both
options.why: Overlapping lists are normal and are not an error.

explanation: Precedence decides scalar keys. List keys merge across levels, which is how teams and individuals both add permissions. A few model-list keys follow their own rules (`fallbackModel`, `modelPicker`, managed `availableModels`, `modelSettings`). To take away something a lower file allows, write an `ask` or `deny` rule, because those are evaluated before `allow`.
reference: Claude Code docs: Settings files and precedence (Lists merge instead of overriding)

stem: Your `~/.claude/settings.json` sets `"model": "opus"`, the project's `.claude/settings.json` sets `"model": "sonnet"`, and your shell profile exports `ANTHROPIC_MODEL=haiku`. There are no managed settings. You run plain `claude` with no flags. Which model does the session start on?

options.text: Sonnet, because shared project settings beat user settings
options.why: That is right between the two files, but the exported variable overrides the `model` key from any file.

options.text: Opus, because your personal settings follow you everywhere
options.why: User settings are the lowest file level, and the environment variable beats them anyway.

options.text: Haiku, because `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` overrides the `model` setting in every file
options.why: The docs list `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` above the `model` setting. Only `/model` in the session or `--model` at launch would beat it.

options.text: Claude Code refuses to start and asks you to resolve the conflicting values in the three places
options.why: Conflicting values are normal, and precedence rules settle them.

explanation: Environment variables are not a level in the settings stack; each variable/key pair has its own rule. For the model, the priority is `/model` during the session, then `--model`, then `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, then the `model` setting, then `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL` (which applies only when no file sets `model`). A stray `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` in a shell profile is a common reason a team's pinned model is ignored.
reference: Claude Code docs: Model configuration (Setting your model); Settings files and precedence

stem: A teammate adds a `// why we deny curl` comment above a deny rule in the committed `.claude/settings.json`. Interactive sessions show a dialog at start-up, but the nightly `claude -p` job runs normally and Claude happily uses `curl`. What explains this, and how do you confirm it?

options.text: Settings files are strict JSON; `-p` shows no dialog and skips the broken file, and `claude doctor` reports what was dropped
options.why: The comment is a syntax error. Interactive mode shows a Settings Error dialog, while a `-p` run quietly continues without that file.

options.text: Deny rules are not applied in `-p` mode, so the comment is irrelevant; use `--disallowedTools` in CI
options.why: Deny rules apply in headless runs too. The rules were never loaded because the file failed to parse.

options.text: Comments are allowed, but rules that follow a comment are treated as advisory
options.why: Settings files do not accept comments. `//` and trailing commas are syntax errors.

options.text: Headless runs read `.claude/settings.local.json` instead of `.claude/settings.json`
options.why: Headless runs read the same settings sources. The committed file was skipped because it is invalid.

explanation: If a user, project or local settings file has invalid JSON, interactive sessions show a Settings Error dialog. A single bad entry, such as a malformed permission rule, shows a Settings Warning and only that entry is skipped. A `-p` run shows nothing and continues without the broken file or value, so a security rule can disappear silently in CI. Use `/status` to see which sources loaded, `claude doctor` for details, and the `$schema` line for editor validation.
reference: Claude Code docs: Settings files and precedence (Fix a broken settings file)

stem: A Python Agent SDK service never set `setting_sources`, so it loaded user, project and local settings like the CLI. A developer then adds `skills=["pdf"]`. Since that change, the allow rules in `.claude/settings.local.json` and the notes in `CLAUDE.local.md` no longer apply, while project `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/settings.json` still do. What is the cause and the fix?

options.text: `skills` replaces all filesystem settings with the listed skills; drop `skills` and add `"Skill"` to `allowed_tools`
options.why: Project settings still load, so nothing replaced everything. Adding `"Skill"` by hand is also the deprecated approach.

options.text: Local files are read only in interactive sessions; move the rules into `.claude/settings.json`
options.why: The SDK reads local settings whenever the `local` source is enabled, and it was enabled before this change.

options.text: When `skills` is set and `setting_sources` is not, Python fills in `["user", "project"]`; list all three
options.why: The Python transport fills in `["user", "project"]` so skills are discovered, which quietly drops `local`.

options.text: The skills allowlist also filters CLAUDE files, so `CLAUDE.local.md` needs a `skills` entry
options.why: The list filters which skills the model may invoke. It has nothing to do with CLAUDE files or permission rules.

explanation: In `claude_agent_sdk` 0.2.172, setting `skills` makes the transport add the Skill tool rule and, if `setting_sources` is `None`, set it to `["user", "project"]`. Unset `setting_sources` normally means all three sources, so adding `skills` silently removes the `local` layer (`CLAUDE.local.md`, `settings.local.json`). The TypeScript SDK does not narrow sources this way. Any code that depends on specific sources should set them explicitly: `setting_sources=["user", "project", "local"]`.
reference: claude_agent_sdk (Python) 0.2.172 source: SubprocessCLITransport._apply_skills_defaults; Agent SDK docs: Extend agents with skills

stem: Security wants Claude Code to never run `curl` on any developer laptop, in every repository, and developers must not be able to undo it. A platform engineer proposes four approaches. Which one meets every requirement?

options.text: A managed `CLAUDE.md` saying "Never run curl", which `claudeMdExcludes` cannot remove
options.why: It cannot be excluded, but CLAUDE.md is guidance Claude tries to follow, not enforcement. Claude can still run `curl`.

options.text: A `Bash(curl *)` rule in `permissions.deny` in managed settings
options.why: The client enforces managed deny rules whatever Claude decides, and nothing in user, project, local or `--settings` can override them.

options.text: A `Bash(curl *)` deny rule committed to every repository's `.claude/settings.json`
options.why: This enforces in repos that have the file, but it misses new repos and anyone can edit or delete the committed file.

options.text: A deny rule pushed into each developer's `~/.claude/settings.json` by a setup script
options.why: Developers own their user settings and can delete the rule.

explanation: The docs split the two cleanly. Managed settings handle technical enforcement (`permissions.deny`, `sandbox.enabled`, login restrictions). A managed CLAUDE.md handles behavioural guidance (style, compliance reminders). If an interview answer relies on CLAUDE.md for a hard rule, call it out as advisory. Pair the managed deny with a managed CLAUDE.md line if you also want Claude to explain the policy to developers.
reference: Claude Code docs: How Claude remembers your project (Manage CLAUDE.md for large teams); Settings files and precedence

stem:
A `fix-lint` skill starts with:

```markdown
## Current lint errors
!`npm run lint`

Fix every error listed above.
```

It works on a clean tree, but whenever there are lint errors (exactly when you need it), invoking it shows `Shell command failed for pattern "!`npm run lint`"` and Claude does nothing. The command is already allowed. What is happening, and what is the smallest fix?

options.text: The injected command needs approval; add `allowed-tools: Bash(npm run lint)` to the frontmatter
options.why: A permission problem gives a different message: `Shell command permission check failed`. This command was allowed and ran.

options.text: Claude received the error text instead of the lint output; tell it in the skill body to run the linter itself
options.why: Claude receives nothing. A failed injected command aborts the whole invocation before any skill content is sent.

options.text: Injected commands cannot run npm scripts; move the command into a `PreToolUse` hook
options.why: Any shell command can be injected. A hook is the wrong tool for gathering context at invocation time.

options.text: Lint exits non-zero when it finds errors, which aborts the invocation; change the line to ``!`npm run lint || true` ``
options.why: With the default bash shell, any non-zero exit counts as a failure. `|| true` keeps the output and stops the abort.

explanation: Injected commands are all-or-nothing. A failure aborts the entire skill invocation, and the error includes the command's output. Exit code 1 is treated as normal only for search and comparison commands such as `grep` and `diff`. Exit codes of 2 or higher always fail. For check scripts that signal problems through the exit code, append `|| true`. Remember that stderr is merged into stdout, so the lint messages still reach Claude.
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills (When an injected command fails)

stem: Your CI runs `claude -p` against pull requests from outside contributors, in a checkout nobody has ever trusted interactively. A contributor's PR adds `.claude/skills/helper/SKILL.md`. Which risks from that file are real? (Choose two.)

options.text: Its `allowed-tools` frontmatter takes effect even though the folder was never trusted
options.why: The docs state that workspace trust does not gate `allowed-tools`, even in a `-p` run in an untrusted folder.

options.text: When the skill is invoked, its `!` commands can run on the runner before Claude reads anything, if its own `allowed-tools` pre-approves them
options.why: Injected commands run while the skill renders. They are checked against permission rules, and `allowed-tools` counts as a pre-approval.

options.text: None: project skills stay inactive until someone enables them in the `/skills` menu
options.why: Project skills are discovered automatically. The `/skills` menu only adjusts visibility.

options.text: None, if the skill sets `disable-model-invocation: true`, because its commands then never run
options.why: That flag stops Claude from invoking the skill on its own. A user or prompt that sends `/helper` still runs it, commands included.

options.text: It can silently override the deny rules in your managed settings
options.why: Deny rules still take precedence over a skill's `allowed-tools`, and managed rules cannot be overridden.

explanation: Treat repository skills as code. For untrusted input, the mitigations are: review `.claude/` changes before running Claude on them, turn off the `project` source for that run, set `disableSkillShellExecution` (replaces injected commands with a placeholder for user, project, plugin and added-directory skills), or have the org set `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`, which makes Claude Code ignore `allowed-tools` in project and personal skills. Run the job in an isolated sandbox with no secrets it does not need.
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills (Pre-approve tools; Permission checks on injected commands)

stem: In a long session you invoked a 9,000-token `migration-playbook` skill early on, then nine other skills later. After auto-compaction, Claude stops following the playbook's rules, which sit near the end of its `SKILL.md`. What explains this, and what is the best structural fix?

options.text: Compaction never keeps any skill bodies at all; move the whole playbook into the root `CLAUDE.md` so it survives
options.why: Skill bodies are re-attached within a budget. Putting 9,000 tokens in CLAUDE.md would cost them in every session.

options.text: Re-attached skills keep only their first 5,000 tokens within a 25,000 budget; move key rules to the top
options.why: Truncation keeps the start of the file, and older invocations lose out to newer ones. Front-load key rules, keep the body short, and re-invoke if needed.

options.text: Claude Code re-reads `SKILL.md` from disk every turn, and a background edit changed the file
options.why: Claude Code does not re-read a skill on later turns. The rendered content enters the conversation once.

options.text: The skill's `allowed-tools` grant expired, and an expired grant also removes its instructions
options.why: Grants and instructions have separate lifecycles. A grant ending never removes instructions.

explanation: After summarization, Claude Code re-attaches the most recent invocation of each skill, keeping the first 5,000 tokens of each, within a combined 25,000-token budget filled from the most recently invoked skill. A big skill invoked long ago is the first to be truncated or dropped. Put the most important instructions near the top of `SKILL.md`, move detail into supporting files, and invoke the skill again when you return to that work.
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills (Skill content lifecycle); Explore the context window

stem: A 12-person team's root `CLAUDE.md` has grown to 600 lines: frontend rules, Terraform conventions, a release runbook, a directory-by-directory tour, and the core build and test commands. Claude has started ignoring rules. Which changes reduce what loads in every session while keeping the guidance available? (Choose three.)

options.text: Move the frontend and Terraform sections into `.claude/rules/` files with `paths` frontmatter
options.why: Path-scoped rules load only when Claude works on matching files.

options.text: Turn the release runbook into a skill with `disable-model-invocation: true`
options.why: A multi-step procedure belongs in a skill. With that flag even its description stays out of context until someone runs it.

options.text: Delete the directory-by-directory tour
options.why: Claude can work out the layout by reading the code, and the docs list file-by-file descriptions as content to exclude.

options.text: Split the file into five `@import`ed topic files
options.why: Imports load at launch with the importing file, so the context cost stays the same.

options.text: Prefix every rule with "IMPORTANT"
options.why: When everything is emphasised, nothing stands out. The docs suggest emphasis only for a single rule that keeps being skipped.

options.text: Move everything into each developer's `CLAUDE.local.md`
options.why: It still loads every session, it fragments the team's guidance across 12 private copies, and it is not version-controlled.

explanation: Keep the root file to facts every session needs: commands, conventions, "always do X" rules. Load the rest on demand: path-scoped rules or subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` files for areas of the codebase, skills for procedures, and nothing at all for what Claude can derive from the code. Anything that must happen without exception belongs in a hook. `/doctor` can propose these cuts for a checked-in CLAUDE.md.
reference: Claude Code docs: Best practices; How Claude remembers your project

stem: A `write-changelog` skill uses `context: fork` and `agent: Explore`. Its body says "Write a changelog entry for the decisions we made in this conversation, following our CLAUDE.md conventions." The output is generic: it misses the decisions and ignores the conventions. Which change fixes both problems?

options.text: Change `agent: Explore` to `agent: general-purpose` so the subagent loads CLAUDE.md
options.why: This may bring CLAUDE.md into the subagent's startup context, but a `context: fork` subagent still never sees your conversation.

options.text: Add `background: false` so the skill waits for the forked result
options.why: This changes when the result arrives, not what the subagent can see.

options.text: Remove `context: fork` so the skill runs inline in the main conversation
options.why: Inline, the skill's instructions are added to the current conversation, which already has the discussion history and the loaded CLAUDE.md.

options.text: Add `allowed-tools: Read` so the subagent can read the transcript
options.why: The subagent cannot see your conversation, and pre-approving Read does not give it the history or the decisions.

explanation: Despite its name, `context: fork` does not fork the conversation. It starts a fresh subagent of the `agent` type whose prompt is the skill body. Explore and Plan also start without CLAUDE.md, to keep their context small. Use `context: fork` for self-contained tasks with explicit instructions. When the task depends on what was said, run the skill inline (or fork the conversation itself).
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills (Run skills in a subagent)

stem: You launch Claude Code in `repo/packages/api`. These instruction files exist, and all of them load at launch. Claude Code concatenates them rather than letting one override another. Put them in the order they appear in context, first to last.

options.text: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
`repo/CLAUDE.md`
`repo/CLAUDE.local.md`
`repo/packages/api/CLAUDE.md`

explanation: Load order goes from broadest scope to most specific: managed, then user, then the project tree from the root down to the working directory, with `CLAUDE.local.md` appended after `CLAUDE.md` in each directory. So instructions closest to where you launched are read last. Nothing gives one file hard precedence, so if two files contradict each other Claude may follow either. Remove the conflict, or say explicitly in the more specific file that it overrides.
reference: Claude Code docs: How Claude remembers your project (How CLAUDE.md files load)

stem: Your team commits `.claude/skills/code-review/SKILL.md` encoding house review rules. Developers who type `/code-review` get the house version, but those who type `/review` still get the generic bundled review. Why, and how do you stop the generic bundled review from running?

options.text: A project skill replaces the bundled command but not its aliases, so `/review` reaches the bundled skill; deny `Skill(review)`, which blocks the bundled one via its alias
options.why: Same-name skills replace bundled commands, not their aliases. A deny rule naming the alias blocks the bundled skill, leaving the house one.

options.text: Bundled skills always beat project skills; rename the house skill to `team-review`
options.why: A project skill does replace the bundled `/code-review`, as the developers who type that name see. Renaming leaves `/review` unchanged.

options.text: `/review` is a separate built-in; add `"review": "off"` to `skillOverrides` in `.claude/settings.json`
options.why: In project settings, `skillOverrides` matches skill names only. An entry for `review` does not reach the bundled skill through its alias.

options.text: Aliases resolve to personal skills only; move the house skill to each developer's `~/.claude/skills/`
options.why: Aliases belong to the bundled command, wherever your skill lives. A personal copy replaces `/code-review` too, but `/review` still reaches the bundled skill.

explanation: The resolution table: a skill at the enterprise, personal or project level with the same name replaces a bundled skill or built-in command, but not its aliases. Deny rules behave differently: a deny that names an alias, `Skill(review)`, blocks the bundled `/code-review` through that alias, so `/review` stops reaching it and developers learn to use `/code-review`. Interviewers use this to see whether you know the difference between a command's name and the routes that reach it.
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills (Resolve skills that share a name; Restrict Claude's skill access)

stem: An organisation has three requirements. (1) Skills from repositories, plugins and personal folders must stay usable as prompt instructions. (2) Their `` !`command` `` lines must never execute on developer machines. (3) Developers cannot turn this back on. Which control satisfies all three?

options.text: Add `Skill` to `permissions.deny` in managed settings
options.why: This blocks Claude from invoking skills at all, which fails requirement 1.

options.text: Set `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` in managed settings
options.why: Skills' `allowed-tools` are then ignored, but injected commands that a managed rule allows still run, and those that are not allowed abort the whole skill, which fails 1 and 2.

options.text: Set `"disableSkillShellExecution": true` in managed settings
options.why: Each injected command becomes the text `[shell command execution disabled by policy]` while the rest of the skill loads. Managed settings cannot be overridden by users.

options.text: Require `disable-model-invocation: true` in every skill through code review
options.why: A user who types the command still runs the skill and its injected commands. Review-based rules can also be bypassed.

explanation: `disableSkillShellExecution` covers skills and custom commands from user, project, plugin and additional-directory sources. Bundled and managed skills are not affected, so admins can still ship trusted skills that inject context. The docs call out managed settings as the place where this setting is most useful, because users cannot override it there.
reference: Claude Code docs: Extend Claude with skills (Inject dynamic context)

stem: An internal code-Q&A agent runs on the Agent SDK with `tools: ["Read", "Grep", "Glob"]` and default setting sources. Users correct it repeatedly ("we use pnpm, not npm"), but the agent never remembers these corrections in later sessions, while the same repo in interactive Claude Code builds up auto memory fine. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Auto memory is a CLI-only feature and is never loaded in SDK sessions
options.why: The SDK loads auto memory from `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/` at session start, whatever `settingSources` says.

options.text: Default setting sources leave out `"user"`, which auto memory needs
options.why: Default sources include user, project and local. Auto memory is not controlled by `settingSources` anyway.

options.text: Each SDK session gets a random project directory, so its auto memory folder is different every time it starts
options.why: The memory directory is derived from the git repository, so every session in the same repo shares one folder.

options.text: The agent saves memories with the standard Write and Edit tools, and this tool list leaves both out
options.why: There is no dedicated memory tool. Without Write or Edit, Claude can read existing memory but never save new notes.

explanation: In the SDK, auto memory loads regardless of `settingSources`. To turn it off, set `autoMemoryEnabled: false` or pass `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1` in `env`. Saving new memories requires Write and Edit. For a read-only agent that must learn, either allow Write and Edit scoped to the memory directory, or keep corrections in a curated CLAUDE.md that the agent loads. For multi-tenant hosts, disable auto memory so one tenant's notes cannot leak into another tenant's sessions.
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Use Claude Code features in the SDK (What settingSources does not control)

stem: A TypeScript SDK job passes `plugins: [{ type: "local", path: "~/plugins/review-kit" }]`. The job completes with a `success` result and no error, but `/review-kit:check` never runs; Claude just answers the prompt as plain text. The plugin works when loaded with `claude --plugin-dir`. What is the likely cause, and where should the job have caught it?

options.text: The SDK does not expand `~`, so the path does not exist and the plugin is skipped; check the init message's `plugins` list and `plugin_errors`
options.why: A nonexistent plugin path is skipped and the session continues, so the init message is where the failure shows.

options.text: SDK plugins need `settingSources: ["project"]`; the job should have thrown at start-up
options.why: Plugins load from the paths you pass, independent of setting sources, and a bad path does not throw.

options.text: Plugin skills must also be listed in `skills`; Claude Code would print a warning to stderr
options.why: Leaving out `skills` keeps the CLI defaults, and dispatching `/name` does not depend on the `skills` list anyway.

options.text: Local plugins need a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` manifest; the result would carry an error subtype
options.why: The manifest is optional, since components are found from the directory layout. And the plugin works with `--plugin-dir`.

explanation: SDK plugin paths can be absolute or relative to `cwd`, but `~` is not expanded. Build the path with `os.homedir()`. A missing directory does not fail the query, and an unmatched `/name` is sent to Claude as an ordinary message. So assert on the `system`/`init` message in production code: is the plugin in `plugins`, is anything in `plugin_errors`, and does `skills` or `slash_commands` contain `review-kit:check`?
reference: Claude Agent SDK docs: Plugins in the SDK (Troubleshooting); Extend agents with skills (Dispatch commands by name)
